note: The Question Genome. Most exam questions are not new — they are familiar ideas with one important change. Families come in three kinds, validated against 70 real exam questions in research/exam-genome-audit.md: MUTATION (same problem, examiner changes the conditions — ask 'what changed?'), METHOD (same goal, competing tools — ask 'which instrument, and what told you?'), and RECALL (a fixed catalogue to reproduce — ask 'can you state and prove it?'). 'steps' are what the question always asks of you. 'operators' are the shared vocabulary of what an examiner can change; 'loadBearing' marks the one that actually creates the difficulty, which is rarely all of them. 'order' is the EVOLUTION order.

6.2.name: Partial fractions
6.2.core: Split a rational function into pieces you already know how to integrate.

6.2-partial-fractions-distinct-linear.changed: Nothing yet — this is the family in its plainest form.

6.2-partial-fractions-setup-long-divisio.changed: The numerator got heavier than the denominator, so a division appears before the real question starts.

6.2-partial-fractions-repeated-linear.changed: A factor now repeats, so it earns one term per power instead of one term.

6.2-partial-fractions-irreducible-quadra.changed: A factor stopped being factorable, so its numerator becomes linear — and an arctangent appears at the end.

6.2-partial-fractions-repeated-quadratic.changed: Both mutations at once: a quadratic factor that also repeats.

6.2-partial-fractions-complete-square-fi.changed: The quadratic is disguised — you must complete the square before you can even read the denominator.

steps.label: Make it proper
steps.text: If the top is as heavy as the bottom, divide first — everything downstream assumes a proper fraction.

steps.label: Read the denominator
steps.text: The factor structure decides the whole shape of the answer before any algebra begins.

steps.label: Choose the template
steps.text: One term per distinct linear factor, one per power of a repeated factor, a linear numerator over each quadratic.

steps.label: Find the constants
steps.text: Cover-up, substitution of convenient values, or equating coefficients.

steps.label: Integrate each piece
steps.text: Logarithms from linear factors, powers from repeated ones, arctangent from quadratics.

steps.label: Finish honestly
steps.text: Absolute values inside logarithms, and the constant of integration.

6.2.evidence: 1 real question (2011b A3) — the exam reaches for this less often than the textbook does, but when it does it arrives with both a repeated factor and an irreducible quadratic at once.

9.6.name: Taylor approximation
9.6.core: Rebuild a function near a point from what it does at that point.

9.6-taylor-maclaurin-definition-coeffici.changed: Nothing yet — the polynomial is built straight from the definition.

9.6-standard-maclaurin-table-recall.changed: The derivatives are no longer computed; they are recalled. Speed replaces derivation.

9.6-building-new-series-substitution.changed: You start from a series you already own and transform it rather than beginning again.

9.6-series-via-long-division.changed: No closed form exists, so the terms must be ground out by division.

9.6-analytic-functions-remainder.changed: The question stops asking for the polynomial and starts asking how wrong it is.

steps.label: Choose the expansion point
steps.text: Almost always 0, but a question can move it — and everything shifts with it.

steps.label: Generate the polynomial
steps.text: From the definition, from the standard table, or by transforming a series you already know.

steps.label: Use it
steps.text: Substitute, or feed the expansion into a limit and watch the low-order terms decide the answer.

steps.label: Bound the error
steps.text: A polynomial is a promise with a range; the remainder term says how far the promise holds.

steps.label: Say what it means
steps.text: How many terms are needed, whether it converges, what happens as x grows.

9.6.evidence: 10 citations, 9 of them the opening Taylor-limit. The audit found the numerator is often reused verbatim between sittings while the denominator goes one order deeper.

9.3.name: Convergence tests
9.3.core: One unchanging question — does this series converge? — and six instruments to answer it.

steps.label: Read the shape
steps.text: Factorials and n-th powers point one way; rational and logarithmic terms point another.

steps.label: Pick the instrument
steps.text: The cheapest test that can settle it, not the most powerful one.

steps.label: Apply it cleanly
steps.text: Compute the limit or the comparison the test actually requires.

steps.label: Say what settled it
steps.text: A convergence claim without the test that produced it earns nothing.

9.3-integral-test.changed: Wins when the terms are a decreasing function you can actually integrate — and it delivers the p-series outright.

9.3-direct-comparison-test.changed: Wins when you already know a neighbouring series and the inequality points the right way.

9.3-limit-comparison-test.changed: Wins when the inequality is awkward but the asymptotic behaviour is obvious.

9.3-ratio-test.changed: Wins on factorials and products, where consecutive terms simplify.

9.3-root-test.changed: Wins on n-th powers, especially exponent towers where the ratio is a mess.

9.3-test-selection.changed: The exam rarely names the test — choosing is the marked skill.

9.3.evidence: 16 citations across all 8 papers — the most-tested family in the course. Every paper asks it in three parts, each part demanding a different instrument.

6.5.name: Improper-integral convergence
6.5.core: Never evaluate it — decide whether it is finite by comparing it with something you already understand.

steps.label: Find where it is improper
steps.text: An infinite limit, a singular point, or — the expensive case — both ends at once.

steps.label: Read the order of the integrand
steps.text: Near the trouble, replace every factor by its leading behaviour: sin u ~ u, 1-cos u ~ u²/2, 1-e^(-u) ~ u.

steps.label: Choose the comparison
steps.text: A p-integral you know converges or diverges, pointing the right way for the inequality.

steps.label: Say what settled it
steps.text: An inequality in the wrong direction proves nothing; asymptotic comparison needs a limit.

6.5-comparison-test.changed: Nothing yet — the plain form. Read the leading order, compare with a p-integral. Seen bare in 2011 A3.

6.5-p-integral-test.changed: The comparison itself becomes the question: for which p does it converge?

6.5-type-1-infinite-interval.changed: The integrand is disguised — a difference of roots, or something needing a series expansion, before its order can be read at all. This is the most common twist on these papers (2010 A3, 2012 A5, 2011b A2).

6.5-type-2-unbounded-integrand.changed: The lower limit becomes 0, so the integral is singular at BOTH ends and must be split. The integrand may look terrifying and be routine; the marks are in the splitting (2020 A5, 2023 A5).

6.5.evidence: 8 of 8 papers carry this family. Blind audit: 1 base, 3 hide-the-structure, 2 change-the-domain, 2 change-the-object.

9.1.name: Recursive sequence limits
9.1.core: Show a recursively defined sequence converges, then find what it converges to.

steps.label: Show it is monotone
steps.text: Induction: assume the step, prove the next one keeps the direction.

steps.label: Show it is bounded
steps.text: Guess the bound from the fixed point, then prove it by induction.

steps.label: Conclude the limit exists
steps.text: Monotone and bounded is the theorem being tested — name it.

steps.label: Solve for the limit
steps.text: Let n→∞ on both sides of the recursion and solve; discard roots the bound forbids.

9.1-sequence-monotonic-bounded-convergen.changed: Nothing yet — and on these papers, almost nothing ever does. 2011 A4 and 2011b A4 are the SAME question with different constants.

9.1-sequence-workhorse-limits.changed: The sequence is given in closed form instead of recursively, so the work moves to standard limits.

9.1-sequence-limit-basic-laws.changed: The limit is assembled from limit laws or the Squeeze Theorem rather than a fixed point.

9.1.evidence: 3 real questions. The audit found this family is dominated by RESKINNING: the sequences differ in constants only. Learn it once and it is done.

9.5.name: Radius of convergence
9.5.core: Find where a power series lives — and then check its two endpoints separately.

steps.label: Test the coefficients
steps.text: Ratio or root test on |a_n|; whichever the coefficient shape makes cheap.

steps.label: Read off the radius
steps.text: The limit gives 1/R — mind whether you computed R or its reciprocal.

steps.label: Test each endpoint
steps.text: Substitute x = ±R and test the resulting number series. This is where the marks hide.

steps.label: State the interval
steps.text: Open, half-open or closed — the endpoints decide, and they can disagree.

9.5-radius-interval-of-convergence-with-.changed: Nothing yet — the plain form. Every paper that asks this asks it in parts, with the last part hardest (2010 A4, 2023 A3, 2023b A3).

9.5-power-series-definition-radius-conce.changed: The coefficients become an exponent tower or a ratio of factorials, so the ratio test must survive n^(n²) and (n!)^5.

9.5-power-series-algebra.changed: Two series are combined first, so the coefficient sequence must be built before it can be tested.

9.5-term-by-term-differentiation-integra.changed: The series is differentiated or integrated term by term — the radius survives, the endpoints may not.

9.5-abels-theorem-continuity.changed: The question moves entirely to the endpoint, where Abel's theorem is the only tool.

9.5.evidence: 3 real questions, all multi-part with an exponent-tower coefficient in the final part.

mutation.note: Same problem; the examiner changed the conditions.

method.prompt: Which instrument, and what told you?
method.note: Same goal; competing tools. The skill is choosing.

recall.prompt: Can you state it, and prove it?
recall.note: A fixed catalogue of results to reproduce. Nothing is being mutated.
